screens.title: Implementing Program Instructions and Logic
screens.subtitle: How instruction handlers, Context, account access, state changes, and custom errors work in Anchor programs

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on how clients call specific functions inside a Solana program, how those functions receive accounts and data, and how you safely change on‑chain state. You will see the core pieces: instruction handlers exposed by Anchor's program macro, the Context struct that carries accounts and program metadata, and how mutable and immutable references control whether an account's data can be changed. We'll walk through a simple counter example that has initialize and increment handlers, show how the msg! macro helps you see runtime logs, and introduce custom error types so your program returns clear, structured failures. This matters because correct account access and validation are the heart of Solana program safety — mistakes like forgetting to mark an account as mutable will cause panics at runtime, and missing validations can open your program to unexpected behavior. By the end you'll know how to write handler functions, access account fields, perform guarded state updates, and return meaningful errors. Think about why validating every external input is critical, and be ready to try the hands‑on activity to implement and test these instructions.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Instruction handlers plus Context and careful validation are the minimal toolkit for safe, maintainable Solana programs. They let you change state, report useful errors, and keep your dApp predictable.

screens.title: Instruction Handlers: What they are and how clients call them
screens.subtitle: Understand instructions as the RPC between client and program

narration.text: An instruction handler is the program function a client calls to perform a specific action on chain. In Anchor, the #[program] macro exposes the public functions in your module so a transaction instruction can target them. When a client builds a transaction it encodes which instruction to run and supplies the accounts and serialized data that the handler needs. Think of an instruction as a remote function call: the client chooses a handler, packages the accounts that will be read or written, and sends the transaction for execution. A concrete example is our counter app: the client sends an initialize instruction to create and set a counter account to zero, then later sends increment instructions to add one to the stored value. A common misconception is that the handler runs with arbitrary access — it does not. Each account must be explicitly supplied by the client and validated by the program. Another pitfall is assuming any function in your Rust module is callable; only those exposed by the #[program] macro become instruction handlers. Key takeaway: design handlers that clearly document required accounts and inputs so clients can construct correct transactions.

keyIdea.title: Instruction handler definition
keyIdea.text: Instruction handlers are public functions exposed by Anchor that clients invoke via transaction instructions to perform on‑chain actions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Instruction Handlers
Definition

What an instruction handler is

A function exposed by Anchor via the program macro that executes when a client includes it in a transaction instruction.

Key points
  • Clients include the instruction in a transaction with the accounts it needs.
  • Only functions in the #[program] module are callable as instructions.
  • Handlers receive a Context struct with typed account references.
Concrete example
pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
  let counter_account = &mut ctx.accounts.counter_account;
  counter_account.count = 0;
  msg!("Counter account initialized with count: {}", counter_account.count);
  Ok(())
}

pub fn increment(ctx: Context<Increment>) -> Result<()> {
  let counter_account = &mut ctx.accounts.counter_account;
  counter_account.count += 1;
  msg!("Counter incremented to: {}", counter_account.count);
  Ok(())
}
Common misconception

Assuming any function is callable as an instruction. Only functions in the program module become instructions.

Key takeaway

Design instruction signatures to clearly list required accounts and their mutability to keep clients correct.

screens.title: The Context struct: typed access to accounts and metadata
screens.subtitle: How Anchor passes accounts, program id, and remaining accounts into handlers

narration.text: Anchor provides a Context struct to every instruction handler. This Context wraps the accounts listed in your corresponding #[derive(Accounts)] struct and supplies typed references such as ctx. accounts. counter_account. Context also contains program metadata like program_id and a remaining_accounts list for advanced flows. The typed access makes it easy to get mutable or immutable references: &mut ctx. accounts. some_account yields a mutable reference when the accounts struct and transaction flagged it as mutable. A practical example is reading and updating a counter field; you fetch the reference from Context and then write to it. An important pitfall is mismatched account expectations: if the accounts struct does not mark an account as mut but you treat it as mutable inside the handler, the program will panic at runtime. Also remember that clients must provide every account your handler expects; an omission will cause the transaction to fail. A useful habit is to keep your Accounts structs minimal and explicitly declare constraints—owner, signer, init—so Anchor can enforce many checks automatically before your logic executes. How might you use remaining_accounts for a cross‑program invocation? Consider that pattern later as you build CPIs.

keyIdea.title: Context basics
keyIdea.text: Context gives typed account references and program metadata. Use it to get mutable or immutable access and to handle advanced remaining accounts when needed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Context struct
Core idea

Context bundles accounts and metadata

Use ctx.accounts to obtain typed references matching your Accounts struct, and check program_id and remaining_accounts when needed.

Practical notes
  • Mutable access requires the account to be declared with #[account(mut)] in the Accounts struct.
  • Anchor checks many constraints automatically, but custom validations often remain necessary.
  • remaining_accounts is useful for CPIs and variable-length account lists.
Example usage
let counter_account = &mut ctx.accounts.counter_account;
counter_account.count = 0;
msg!("Counter initialized: {}", counter_account.count);
// ctx.program_id and ctx.remaining_accounts are also available for advanced flows
Common mistake

Treating an account as mutable without #[account(mut)] will compile but panic at runtime when the change is attempted.

Pro tip

Declare ownership and signer constraints in the Accounts struct so Anchor can automatically enforce them before your logic runs.

screens.title: Initialize instruction: setting up initial state
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of the initialize handler and its effects

narration.text: The initialize instruction is the first operation a client runs to create and set the initial values of an on‑chain account. In the counter example, initialize obtains a mutable reference to the Counter account from ctx. accounts and sets its count field to zero. The handler then emits a message via the msg! macro to aid debugging. This is a common pattern: allocate or ensure an account exists, set initial fields, and log a clear message. When writing initialize, be explicit about constraints in the Accounts struct: require init if the account must be created, set payer if a wallet funds the account, and ensure ownership constraints match your program id. A common confusion is thinking initialize only runs once automatically — the client must include it in a transaction and the Accounts constraints enforce whether the account is already initialized or not. After implementing initialize, run anchor build to catch compilation or type errors, and in later tests assert that the stored count equals zero. A closing question: what constraints will you add to the Accounts struct to guarantee the account is correctly initialized and funded?

keyIdea.title: Initialize pattern
keyIdea.text: Initialize sets starting state and relies on Accounts constraints such as init and payer to ensure the account is created and funded correctly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Initialize Instruction
Code walkthrough
pub fn initialize(ctx: Context<Initialize>) -> Result<()> {
  let counter_account = &mut ctx.accounts.counter_account;
  counter_account.count = 0;
  msg!("Counter account initialized with count: {}", counter_account.count);
  Ok(())
}
This sets the on-chain field and logs the action for visibility in transaction logs.
Explanation & checks
  • Ensure the Accounts struct marks the counter as #[account(init, payer = user, space = ...)] if the handler creates it.
  • Confirm payer and signer constraints so the transaction is valid and the account is funded.
  • Log with msg! so tests and developers can inspect the action in logs.
Example assertion

After initialize, a test should assert that counter_account.count == 0 to verify the initial state.

Misconception

Initialize won't run automatically — a client transaction must call it and supply correct accounts and fees.

screens.title: Increment instruction: guarded state updates and arithmetic
screens.subtitle: How to increment stored values and guard against overflow

narration.text: Increment demonstrates a basic state change: read a mutable account reference, modify a numeric field, and save the result on chain. In practice you must guard modifications with validations. A simple guard ensures you don't increment past the maximum representable value. The example pattern checks if counter_account. count == u64::MAX and, if so, returns a custom overflow error. This both prevents undefined behavior and gives the client feedback about why the transaction failed. After the guard passes, the handler increments the count and emits a msg! log. A common novice mistake is to assume arithmetic overflow will silently wrap; on Solana it's essential to check bounds explicitly or use checked arithmetic. Another important point is atomicity: the entire instruction either succeeds or fails, so partial state changes won't persist. When writing increment, keep validations close to mutation points and return informative errors when checks fail so client UI can present a clear message to users. Increment instruction: guarded state updates and arithmetic means always validate numerical state changes before mutating accounts to avoid overflows and to provide clear error feedback to clients.. In practical terms, how to increment stored values and guard against overflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guarded updates
keyIdea.text: Always validate numerical state changes before mutating accounts to avoid overflows and to provide clear error feedback to clients.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Increment Instruction
Guard pattern
pub fn increment(ctx: Context<Increment>) -> Result<()> {
  let counter_account = &mut ctx.accounts.counter_account;
  if counter_account.count == u64::MAX {
    return Err(MyError::CounterOverflow.into());
  }
  counter_account.count += 1;
  msg!("Counter incremented to: {}", counter_account.count);
  Ok(())
}
Explanation
  • Check bounds before mutation to avoid overflow and to return a clear error variant.
  • Use Anchor errors to convert enum variants into ProgramError for the runtime.
  • Emit msg! after a successful change so logs reflect the new state for debugging.
Misconception

Assuming increment will always succeed. Always plan for edge cases like max value or invalid account data.

Check

After implementing increment, add tests that attempt to increment at max to ensure the error path works as expected.

screens.title: Using msg! for debugging and visibility
screens.subtitle: How logging helps during development and testing

narration.text: The msg! macro is a simple but powerful debugging aid in Solana programs. When you call msg! with a formatted string, the text is written to the transaction logs and is retrievable via the CLI or block explorers during development and tests. Use it sparingly for informative messages like state transitions or critical validation failures. In our counter example, both initialize and increment call msg! to report the current count; this makes it straightforward to correlate transactions and state changes when reviewing logs after running anchor tests. Developers sometimes overuse logging and leave verbose messages in production, so treat msg! as a development tool and remove or minimize non-essential messages in release builds. Another tip: pair msg! logs with structured error returns. If a guard fails and you return a custom error, include a concise msg! log before returning so logs reflect both the diagnostic and the failure reason. Key takeaway: msg! gives you a readable trail of what your instruction did, which accelerates debugging and test verification. Using msg! for debugging and visibility means use msg! to emit human‑readable logs for important state changes and validation failures, aiding debugging and test assertions.. In practical terms, how logging helps during development and testing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

What msg! does

Writes formatted text to transaction logs. Useful during development and for test traceability.

msg!("Counter incremented to: {}", counter_account.count);
msg!("Counter account initialized with count: {}", counter_account.count);
Guidance
  • Log meaningful state changes and important validation failures.
  • Avoid verbose logging in production to reduce noise and cost.
  • Combine msg! with custom errors so logs and failure reasons both exist.
Practical example

Use msg! inside tests to assert that a logged line appears for a successful initialize or increment, improving test diagnostics.

Misuse

Relying on msg! for control flow or user-facing behavior is a mistake; logs are diagnostic, not business logic.

screens.title: Custom Error Handling with Anchor
screens.subtitle: Define and return descriptive errors using #[error_code]

narration.text: Anchor allows you to declare a custom error enum annotated with #[error_code], where each variant can carry a descriptive message via #[msg]. These enums convert into program errors that the runtime understands, letting you return Err(MyError::Variant. into()) from handlers. In the counter example we add a CounterOverflow variant to communicate that an increment attempted to exceed the maximum allowed value. This practice makes failures explicit and machine- and human-readable at the same time. A practical pattern is to validate conditions early in the handler and return the most specific error possible so client code can react appropriately. Avoid returning generic strings or panicking: Anchor's structured errors are easier for frontends and tests to assert against. A common novice approach is to panic on failure; instead, return a converted error so the whole transaction aborts cleanly and the client receives a clear error code and message. Consider what other errors your program might need, such as Unauthorized or InvalidOwner, and define them so your program communicates failure reasons precisely. Custom Error Handling with Anchor means use #[error_code] enums and return errors via .into() so your program fails with descriptive, testable reasons instead of panics.. In practical terms, define and return descriptive errors using #[error_code]. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Structured errors
keyIdea.text: Use #[error_code] enums and return errors via .into() so your program fails with descriptive, testable reasons instead of panics.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Custom Errors
Example enum
#[error_code]
pub enum MyError {
  #[msg("The counter has reached its maximum value.")]
  CounterOverflow,
  #[msg("Unauthorized access to account.")]
  Unauthorized,
}
Return errors from handlers using Err(MyError::Variant.into()).
Benefits
  • Structured error codes make it easy for tests and frontends to handle specific failure modes.
  • Messages provide human-readable context in logs and explorers.
  • Returning errors prevents panics and gives graceful, deterministic failure behavior.
Pro tip

Design error variants for the common edge cases you expect so clients can map them to UI messages easily.

Misconception

Avoid ad-hoc string errors or panics — they make debugging and automated testing brittle.

screens.title: Mutable vs Immutable account access
screens.subtitle: Why #[account(mut)] matters and what can go wrong

narration.text: Accounts accessed through Context can be mutable or immutable depending on how you declare them in the Accounts struct and how the client includes them in the transaction. When you declare #[account(mut)] for a field, Anchor ensures the runtime marks the account writable and your handler receives a mutable reference such as &mut ctx. accounts. name. This lets you change stored fields. If you forget to mark an account mut but attempt mutation, the program will panic at runtime because the runtime enforces write permissions. A common beginner mistake is adding mut only in the handler and not in the Accounts definition. Another important contrast is read-only accounts: they are safe for checks, signatures, and reads without side effects. For sensitive operations like transfers or state updates, prefer explicit mut annotations and require signer constraints where appropriate. Tests should include negative cases that attempt to mutate a read-only account to ensure your constraints are enforced. In short, mutability is a contract between the transaction and the runtime; your code must honor and declare it before doing any writes. Mutable vs Immutable account access means declaring #[account(mut)] is essential when you intend to write to an account. without it, runtime write permission is denied and your program can panic.. In practical terms, why #[account(mut)] matters and what can go wrong. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mutability contract
keyIdea.text: Declaring #[account(mut)] is essential when you intend to write to an account. Without it, runtime write permission is denied and your program can panic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Mut vs Read-only
Mutable access

#[account(mut)]

Grants write permission and yields &mut references in handlers so you can change account data.

Remember to mark mut in the Accounts struct, not only in handler code.
Immutable access

Read-only accounts

Safe for checks and reading fields. Trying to mutate them causes a runtime error because transaction flags do not permit writes.

Check

Write tests that attempt forbidden mutations to confirm Anchor enforces mutability constraints.

screens.title: Validation patterns: check everything on-chain
screens.subtitle: Verify ownership, signer status, and data invariants

narration.text: Validation is essential for program security. Anchor helps by enforcing many constraints through #[account] attributes, such as signer, owner, init, and seeds. But you still need custom validations inside handlers. Common checks include verifying an account's owner equals the expected program id, ensuring the signer matches an authorized key, and testing numeric ranges before mutations. For example, before decrementing or transferring values you should check that the actor is authorized and the account has sufficient balance or capacity. A frequent mistake is trusting the client or a previous instruction; always perform the check in the handler that does the state change. Tests should validate both success and failure paths so you know which error variant is returned when a validation fails. Organize validations near the top of your handler and return specific errors early to keep logic clear and to prevent accidental state changes under invalid conditions. The closing question: which invariants matter most in your application and how will you test them? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and assessment checks
screens.subtitle: Questions, pitfalls, and how to verify your work

narration.text: Before concluding, let's review common pitfalls and assessment checks you should run. One frequent error is forgetting #[account(mut)] when you plan to modify an account; the symptom is a runtime panic when your handler attempts a write. Another is failing to validate ownership or signer flags, which can allow unintended actors to cause state changes. When adding custom errors, avoid panicking and instead return Err(MyError::Variant. into()) so the transaction aborts cleanly with a meaningful error. For verification, ask these assessment questions: If you want to modify an account inside a handler which Accounts attribute must you set? The correct answer is #[account(mut)]. For custom errors, the right way to return an Anchor error is Err(MyError::Variant. into()). Also verify your tests: add a test that attempts an overflow increment and assert it returns the CounterOverflow error. Finally, check msg! logs during test runs to see the sequence of actions. These checks ensure your program behaves predictably under expected and edge conditions. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the core concepts to retain. Instruction handlers are the callable functions a client targets via transactions. The Context struct provides typed access to accounts and program metadata. Account access must be declared correctly—use #[account(mut)] when you will write data. Use msg! to emit logs that aid development and testing. Finally, implement custom errors with #[error_code] and return them with. into() so failures are descriptive and testable. These practices form the foundation of secure, maintainable Anchor programs: explicit account contracts, early validations, and structured errors. As you move to testing and CPIs, these same principles will guide safe interactions with other programs and users. Consider which errors and checks your next program will need and how to document the required account set so clients can construct correct transactions. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
Instruction Handler
A callable program function invoked by client transactions to change or read state.
Context Struct
Provides typed access to accounts, program_id, and remaining_accounts for handlers.
Account Access
Declare mut for writable accounts and validate ownership and signer constraints.
State Manipulation
Modify account fields via mutable refs; changes are committed if the instruction succeeds.
msg! Macro
Emit transaction logs for debugging and test verification.
Custom Errors
Use #[error_code] enums and return .into() for clear, testable failure reasons.
Summary takeaway

Explicit account contracts, validation, and structured errors make your program safer and your tests reliable.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact concepts to carry forward

narration.text: Keep these three ideas front of mind. First, the Context struct is the typed bridge between transactions and handler code — use it to get mutable or immutable account references and access program metadata. Second, always validate: declare mut where needed, confirm ownership and signer flags, and check numeric boundaries before updating state. Third, return structured errors with Anchor's error macros so clients and tests can identify precise failure reasons. Together these habits reduce runtime surprises and make debugging and testing much simpler. As you implement features, ask: which accounts are required, which must be writable, and what error conditions should be returned? That simple checklist will guide correct design and safer programs. What to Remember means context, explicit validation, and structured errors are essential building blocks for safe anchor programs.. In practical terms, three compact concepts to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What to Remember
Context
Typed access to accounts and program metadata used by handlers.
Validation
Declare mut, check ownership and signer flags, and validate invariants before mutations.
Structured Errors
Define #[error_code] enums and return errors via .into() for clear client feedback.
Final takeaway

Design handlers with explicit account contracts, validate inputs on‑chain, and return clear, structured errors so your program behaves predictably and is easy to test.

ai_generation_note: Create a 10-minute live coding video. Start with the `lib.rs` from the previous chapter that defines the `Counter` struct and the `Initialize`/`Increment` contexts. Focus on implementing the `initialize` and `increment` instruction handler functions. Show how to access `ctx.accounts.counter_account` and modify its `count` field. Demonstrate the `msg!` macro and how its output appears in the terminal during testing (mentioning it's visible in logs). Then, introduce custom error handling by adding the `MyError` enum and implementing the `CounterOverflow` check in the `increment` function. Show how to return `Err(MyError::CounterOverflow.into())`. Use a split-screen view: Rust code on the left, conceptual flow diagram for instruction execution on the right. Include a short reflection prompt: "Think of another custom error you might add to this counter program and why it would be useful."
